 Q1 (a) 5 Marks CO-1 · BL-L Answer length: ~1–1.5 pages

 Explain challenges in maintaining Legacy software.


 Legacy software is older software that was developed decades ago, has been continually modified to meet changes in
 business requirements and computing platforms, and is still business-critical — the organisation cannot simply throw it
 away (Pressman).


Legacy systems are often characterised by poor quality: inextensible designs, convoluted code, poor or non-existent
documentation, and test cases/results that were never archived. Maintaining them is therefore difficult for the following
reasons:

 1. Poor or missing documentation – original design documents are lost or outdated; maintainers must reverse-engineer the
 logic from code.

 2. Obsolete technology – written in old languages (COBOL, FORTRAN, old C) and run on old hardware/OS; skilled
 programmers are rare and expensive.

 3. Convoluted, 'spaghetti' code – years of patches have destroyed the original structure (high coupling, low cohesion), so
 every change risks a side-effect (the ripple effect).
 4. Original developers have left – domain and design knowledge has walked out of the door; nobody fully understands the
 system.

 5. Integration problems – it must interoperate with modern databases, web/mobile front-ends and cloud services for which
 it was never designed.

 6. High cost and risk of change – the system is business-critical, so downtime or a regression is unacceptable; testing is hard
 because test suites were never archived.

 7. Software deterioration – each change introduces new defects before earlier ones are removed, so the failure-rate curve
 keeps rising (software does not wear out, it deteriorates).

When must legacy software evolve? (Pressman) – when it must be adapted to a new computing environment/technology,
enhanced to implement new business requirements, extended to be interoperable with newer systems/databases, or re-
architected to make it viable in a network/cloud environment.


 Example: A bank's 30-year-old COBOL core-banking system must now serve a UPI mobile app. Adding an API layer is risky
 because the code is undocumented and only two retiring employees understand its batch jobs.


 Scoring tip: Definition (1 M) + 5–6 challenges (3 M) + 'why it must evolve' / example (1 M).

 What are the different types of relationships used in class diagrams? Explain with suitable examples.


A class diagram shows the static structure of a system — classes, their attributes/operations and the relationships among
them. The relationships are:

 1. Association – a structural link between two classes whose objects know about each other. Drawn as a solid line with
 optional name, role names and multiplicity (1, 0..1, *, 1..*). Eg: Student enrolls in Course (many-to-many).

 2. Aggregation – a weak 'whole–part' (has-a) association; the part can exist independently of the whole. Hollow diamond at
 the whole end. Eg: Department ◇— Professor (professor exists even if department closes).

 Q1 (d) 5 Marks CO-4 · BL-L Answer length: ~1–1.5 pages

 Explain Unit testing with suitable example.


 Unit testing focuses verification effort on the smallest unit of software design — the component or module (a function,
 method or class). It is white-box oriented and is usually done by the developer.


What is tested in a unit (Pressman's unit-test considerations):

 Module interface – data properly flows in and out (number, order and types of parameters).

 Local data structures – data stored temporarily keeps its integrity (initialisation, types).

 Independent paths – every basis path through the control structure is executed at least once.

 Boundary conditions – the module works correctly at limits (n-1, n, n+1; first/last element; max/min).

 Error-handling paths – all error paths are exercised and messages are meaningful.

Unit-test environment: since a module is not a standalone program, a driver (a 'main program' that accepts test-case data,
passes it to the unit and prints results) and stubs (dummy sub-programs that replace modules called by the unit) are written.

Phases of the Waterfall model

 1. Communication – project initiation and requirements gathering: meetings with the customer and stakeholders to
 understand objectives; output is the Software Requirements Specification (SRS), reviewed and signed off.

 2. Planning – estimating effort and cost, scheduling tasks, identifying risks and resources, and defining how progress will be
 tracked; output is the project plan.

 3. Modeling – analysis (data, functional and behavioural models of the requirements) and design (architecture, data
 structures, interfaces and component-level/algorithmic detail); output is the design document.

 4. Construction – code generation (translating design into source code) and testing (unit, integration and system testing) to
 uncover errors.

 5. Deployment – delivery of the product to the customer, support (maintenance: corrective, adaptive, perfective) and
 collection of feedback.

Variant: the V-model depicts the relationship of quality-assurance actions to these phases — as the team moves down the left
side, requirements are refined into detail; moving up the right side, each level of testing validates the corresponding model
(unit test ↔ component design, integration test ↔ architecture, system test ↔ requirements, acceptance test ↔ customer
needs).

Why the Waterfall model is a prescriptive process model

A prescriptive process model 'prescribes' a set of process elements — framework activities, software engineering actions,
tasks, work products, quality-assurance and change-control mechanisms — and a workflow (the order in which these
elements are inter-related). Its goal is to bring order and structure to software development. Waterfall is the purest example
because:

 1. Fixed, predefined sequence: it prescribes a strict linear flow – communication → planning → modeling → construction →
 deployment; a phase starts only after the previous one is complete and signed off.

 2. Defined work products at each phase: SRS, project plan, design document, code, test reports – each acts as a formal
 'gate' (milestone).

 3. Heavy documentation and formality: process is document-driven; documentation is the main means of communication
 and control.

 4. Plan-driven: scope, schedule and cost are fixed early; deviations are handled through formal change control.

 5. Emphasis on predictability and control rather than adaptability – the defining feature of the prescriptive (vs. agile) family.

 Q3 (a) 10 Marks CO-2 · BL-H Answer length: ~2.5–3.5 pages + diagram

 Define the three key roles in the Scrum framework and mention their core responsibilities.


 Scrum is an agile process framework (Schwaber & Beedle) in which work is done in short, time-boxed iterations called
 sprints (typically 2–4 weeks) by a small, self-organising, cross-functional team, guided by a prioritised product backlog.
 Scrum defines exactly three roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Development Team.


1. Product Owner (PO) — 'the WHAT'

Single person who represents the customer/stakeholders and is accountable for maximising the value of the product.

 Creates, owns and maintains the Product Backlog (features, user stories, bug fixes).

 Prioritises backlog items by business value, risk and dependencies; ensures the backlog is visible and clearly understood.

 Writes user stories with acceptance criteria and clarifies requirements for the team.

 Decides release content and dates; accepts or rejects work at the Sprint Review.

 Acts as the single voice of the customer — only the PO can change backlog priorities.

2. Scrum Master (SM) — 'the HOW of the process'

A servant-leader and facilitator who ensures Scrum is understood and followed; not a project manager.

 Facilitates Scrum events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum (15-minute stand-up), Sprint Review and Retrospective.

 Removes impediments/obstacles reported by the team (e.g., missing hardware, blocked dependency).

 Shields the team from outside interruptions and scope changes during a sprint.

 Coaches the team and the organisation in agile/Scrum practices and self-organisation.

 Helps the PO with backlog management techniques; tracks progress with burn-down charts.

3. Development (Scrum) Team — 'the HOW of building'

A self-organising, cross-functional group of about 3–9 professionals (developers, testers, designers) who turn backlog items
into a potentially shippable increment each sprint.

 Selects items from the product backlog into the Sprint Backlog and estimates effort during sprint planning.

 Decides how to implement the work; collectively accountable (no sub-titles).

 Attends the Daily Scrum answering: What did I do since the last meeting? What obstacles am I facing? What will I do by
 the next meeting?

 Builds, tests and integrates the increment to meet the Definition of Done; demonstrates it at Sprint Review.

 Q3 (b) 10 Marks CO-3 · BL-H Answer length: ~2.5–3.5 pages + diagram

 Critically evaluate the importance of UML in bridging the gap between Object-Oriented Analysis (OOA) and Object-
 Oriented Design (OOD). Provide an example showing how a conceptual model transitions into specific UML diagrams.


OOA answers what the system must do – it models the problem domain in terms of objects, classes, attributes, relationships
and behaviour as seen by the user. OOD answers how – it transforms the analysis model into a blueprint of software classes,
interfaces, subsystems and their collaborations. UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standard, graphical language for
visualising, specifying, constructing and documenting the artifacts of a software system (Booch, Rumbaugh, Jacobson).

Why UML bridges the OOA → OOD gap

 1. One notation for both phases – the same class/sequence/state notation is used in analysis and design, so analysis models
 are refined rather than re-written; no translation loss between analyst and designer.

 2. Seamless, traceable refinement – a conceptual class (Book) becomes a design class (BookCopy with operations, visibility,
 types); each use case traces to sequence diagrams and then to methods. Traceability makes impact-analysis of changes
 easy.

 3. Multiple views – use-case view (requirements), structural view (class/object), behavioural view (sequence, collaboration,
 activity, state) and implementation view (component, deployment) cover all concerns from problem to solution.

 4. Common vocabulary between customers, analysts, designers and testers; diagrams are easier to review than text.

 5. Supports iterative development – models are progressively elaborated in each iteration (Unified Process).

 6. Tool support – CASE tools generate code skeletons from class diagrams and reverse-engineer code into diagrams
 (forward/reverse engineering).

Critical evaluation (limitations)

 UML is a notation, not a method – it does not tell the team how to find good classes or a good architecture.

 Large set of 13+ diagram types → risk of over-modeling and 'documentation for its own sake'; agile teams often draw only
 sketches.

 Models can drift out of sync with code unless maintained (model–code gap).

Data-centered architecture: a data store (file or database) resides at the centre and is accessed frequently by other

data; each filter works independently of upstream/downstream filters, expecting data in a certain form and producing data in

How efficiency defines quality

 Time behaviour – response time, throughput, processing time (e.g., search results in < 2 s).

 Resource behaviour – CPU, memory, battery, bandwidth, storage used.

 An efficient product feels fast, scales to more users per server and costs less to operate; inefficiency directly degrades user

How maintainability defines quality

 Analysability – ease of diagnosing deficiencies or causes of failure.

 Changeability – effort to implement modifications.

 Stability – low risk of unexpected effects after modification.

 Testability – effort to validate the modified software.

 Since most of a product's life-cycle cost is maintenance, high maintainability means faster bug fixes, cheaper

How portability defines quality

 Adaptability – can run in different environments without change (Windows/Linux/cloud, browsers, screen sizes).
 Installability – effort to install in a given environment.

 Conformance – adheres to portability standards/conventions.

 Replaceability – can replace another specified product in that environment.

 A portable product reaches more users and survives platform changes (e.g., a web app that works on any browser, a Java
 app on any JVM).

Overall: ISO 9126 defines quality not as a single value but as a profile across characteristics; efficiency reflects operational
quality, maintainability reflects quality over change, and portability reflects quality across environments. (ISO 9126 has since
been superseded by ISO/IEC 25010, which adds security and compatibility as separate characteristics.)
